title: Charged black holes
one_line_summary: Derives the Reissner-Nordström metric of a static point charge from the Einstein-Maxwell equations, classifies its horizons by the sign of m^2 - epsilon^2, builds an Eddington-Finkelstein-type spacetime diagram from the slopes of null rays, shows that neutral radial geodesics bounce off a repulsive core, and constructs the Kruskal-type maximal extension whose Penrose diagram is an endless chain of universes joined through timelike, avoidable singularities.
role_in_book: Chapter 19 sits between the Schwarzschild black-hole trilogy (ch15 solution, ch17 horizons and Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates, ch18 Kruskal extension and Penrose diagrams) and the Kerr chapter (ch20). It deliberately replays the whole Schwarzschild programme on a metric that is still spherically symmetric and algebraically easy, so that the genuinely new global features that Kerr will also have - an inner horizon, a timelike singularity, a nonstatic band between two horizons, an infinite tower of asymptotic regions and an unstable inner horizon - are met first without the burden of rotation. It also exercises the Maxwell energy-momentum tensor from ch12 as a real gravitational source.

assumed_background.topic: Derivation of the Schwarzschild solution from the canonical static spherically symmetric line element
Birkhoff's theorem for vacuum spherical symmetry
Maxwell tensor F_ab, covariant Maxwell equations and the Maxwell energy-momentum tensor
Trace-free property of the electromagnetic energy-momentum tensor
Derivative of the metric determinant, partial_c g = 2g Gamma^a_ac, which yields the divergence formula for antisymmetric tensors
Geodesic equations from a Lagrangian and first integrals from ignorable coordinates
Coordinate versus intrinsic singularities, Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates, event horizons, and the misleading Schwarzschild-coordinate diagram
Kruskal extension, double null coordinates and Penrose (conformal) diagrams
Coulomb field of a point charge and Gauss's law
Roots and discriminant of a quadratic; sketching rational functions
Integrating first-order ODEs and partial fractions of logarithmic integrals
Energy-diagram reasoning for one-dimensional motion in a potential

learning_objectives: Reader can set up the static, spherically symmetric Einstein-Maxwell problem, justify replacing G_ab by R_ab using the vanishing trace of the Maxwell stress tensor, and state the radial-field ansatz for F_ab.
Reader can carry the Maxwell and field equations through to e^nu = 1 - 2m/r + epsilon^2/r^2 with lambda = -nu, and identify m and epsilon by the Schwarzschild and Coulomb limits.

Reader can locate the horizons r_plus/minus = m +/- sqrt(m^2 - epsilon^2), classify the three cases epsilon^2 < m^2, = m^2, > m^2, and explain why r = 0 is an intrinsic singularity while r = r_plus/minus are coordinate singularities.
Reader can explain why t and r swap timelike/spacelike roles in the band between the horizons and why that band is not static.
Reader can transform to advanced Eddington-Finkelstein-type coordinates, write the two radial null families, and sketch light cones across all three regions using only the graphs of 1+f and 1-f.
Reader can reduce radial neutral geodesics to rdot^2 = u_0^2 - g_00, use g_00 as an effective potential, and show that neutral particles are turned back before reaching r = 0.
Reader can explain why a diagram in which a worldline only approaches r = r_minus asymptotically signals an incomplete coordinate patch, by analogy with the Schwarzschild infall picture.

Reader can construct the tortoise coordinate, the double null coordinates and the exponential Kruskal-type coordinates for the outer horizon, and see why the exponent constant is fixed by the horizon radii.

Reader can read the Penrose diagrams for all three charge-to-mass cases: the infinite ladder of universes, timelike singularities, the extremal chain with degenerate horizons, and the naked-singularity triangle.
Reader can describe the infinite redshift at r_plus for a distant observer, the trapped spheres of region II, and the infinite blueshift and suspected instability at r_minus.

teaching_approach.summary: A compact, derivation-driven replay of the Schwarzschild programme with one extra parameter. Each step is announced as the charged counterpart of something done in chapters 15, 17 or 18, most algebra is deferred to marked exercises, and the physics is extracted from pictures: a plot of g_00 decides the horizon structure and doubles as the potential for radial motion, graphs of 1+f and 1-f give the tilt of light cones, and Penrose diagrams summarize the global structure. The last pages switch from derivation to interpretation, raising wormhole travel, topological identification and inner-horizon blueshift as open or speculative matters.
narrative_arc: Motivate: the charged point mass is worth studying because its structure foreshadows the rotating Kerr solution of the next chapter.
Model: impose spherical symmetry, staticity and asymptotic flatness on the Einstein-Maxwell system and choose a purely radial electric field.
Solve: Maxwell's equations give the field, the Einstein equations force lambda = -nu and a single integrable ODE, yielding the Reissner-Nordström metric.

Check: epsilon -> 0 returns Schwarzschild (fixing m as geometric mass); large r returns the Coulomb field (fixing epsilon as charge); a Birkhoff-type theorem shows staticity was not really an assumption.
Diagnose: factor g_00 through the quadratic Q(r), classify by its discriminant, separate regions I, II, III, and note the swap of coordinate character in II.

Re-coordinatize: follow the Eddington-Finkelstein recipe, obtain straight ingoing rays and a slope formula for outgoing rays, and sketch the spacetime diagram qualitatively; identify r_plus as an event horizon.
Probe with test particles: radial neutral geodesics in the g_00 potential show bounded and unbounded motion and a repulsive core.
Detect incompleteness: a particle reaching r_minus in finite proper time contradicts the asymptotic picture, so the manifold must be extended.
Extend and compactify: tortoise coordinate, double null coordinates, exponential Kruskal-type coordinates, arctan compactification to a Penrose diagram.

Interpret: infinitely many universes, avoidable timelike singularity, one-way wormhole journeys, possible identifications, infinite redshift at r_plus and blueshift at r_minus with a warning about instability.
Close: quote the Penrose diagrams for the extremal and super-extremal cases and send the reader to Hawking and Ellis.
signature_moves: Explicit template reuse: every construction (canonical metric, Birkhoff, Eddington-Finkelstein, Kruskal, Penrose) is introduced as the analogue of its Schwarzschild version, so only the effect of charge is new.
Results stated with '(exercise)' flags: the text records the outcome of each tedious computation and leaves the verification to keyed exercises 19.1-19.17.
Qualitative slope reading: the outgoing null family is never integrated; its slope (1+f)/(1-f) is read from two plotted curves to draw the light cones region by region.
One graph, two jobs: the plot of g_00 against r first displays horizons and regions (Fig. 19.2) and is then reused as an effective potential with horizontal energy lines (Fig. 19.5).
Classification by the discriminant of a quadratic, which turns the physics question 'how many horizons?' into school algebra.
Warning that a smooth-looking diagram can lie, tied back to the Schwarzschild-coordinate infall picture of Fig. 17.7, used to motivate extension.
A staged coordinate ladder t -> tbar -> (v, w) -> (v', w') -> (v'', w''), each rung removing one defect of the previous chart.
Penrose diagrams drawn with t = constant and r = constant grids overlaid on selected blocks, so the reader can see how the familiar static coordinates sit inside the compactified picture.

sections.title: The field of a charged mass point
sections.summary: Frames the Reissner-Nordström solution as a simpler rehearsal of Kerr. Writes the Einstein-Maxwell system, uses the trace-free Maxwell stress tensor to trade G_ab for R_ab, adopts the canonical static spherical line element and a purely radial electric field. Maxwell's equations reduce to one total derivative that fixes E up to a constant, identified as the charge by the Coulomb limit. The 00 and 11 field equations give lambda = -nu, the 22 equation integrates to the RN metric, epsilon = 0 recovers Schwarzschild, and a boxed Birkhoff-type theorem says staticity is automatic.
key_moves: Trace of G_ab = 8 pi T_ab with T^a_a = 0 gives R = 0, so the equivalent system R_ab = 8 pi T_ab can be used (19.2).
Spherical symmetry plus staticity reduce the metric to two functions nu(r), lambda(r) (19.5-19.6).
A charge at rest produces only a radial electric field, so F_ab has a single independent component F_10 = -F_01 = E(r) (19.7).
The homogeneous Maxwell equations hold identically; the divergence equation becomes (e^{-(nu+lambda)/2} r^2 E)' = 0 (19.8), integrated to (19.9).
Asymptotic flatness (19.10) makes E approach epsilon/r^2, which names epsilon as the charge.
Combining the 00 and 11 components gives lambda' + nu' = 0, hence lambda = -nu by the boundary condition (19.11).
The angular (22) component gives (r e^nu)' = 1 - epsilon^2/r^2 (19.12), integrated with a new constant m to (19.13) and the line element (19.14).
epsilon = 0 returns Schwarzschild, fixing m as the geometric mass; the analogue of Birkhoff's theorem is stated without the (longer) proof.

sections.title: Intrinsic and coordinate singularities
sections.summary: Writes g_00 = Q(r)/r^2 with Q a quadratic and uses its discriminant m^2 - epsilon^2 to sort cases. With more charge than mass there are no zeros and only the curvature singularity at r = 0 remains; otherwise Q vanishes at r_plus/minus. Fig. 19.2 contrasts RN and Schwarzschild g_00. For the two-root case the metric is regular in three bands I, II, III separated by null surfaces; t and r swap causal character in band II, which is therefore not static, and the misaligned light cones make the bands look disconnected in these coordinates, motivating Eddington-Finkelstein.
concepts: interchange of timelike and spacelike coordinate character
key_moves: Factor the metric coefficient as Q(r)/r^2 with Q = r^2 - 2mr + epsilon^2 (19.15).
Sign of the discriminant Delta = m^2 - epsilon^2 decides whether Q has zero, one or two positive roots.
The curvature invariant R^abcd R_abcd is cited to certify r = 0 as intrinsic.
Roots r_plus/minus (19.16) are singular only in these coordinates; for epsilon^2 = m^2 they merge and region II disappears.
g_00 changes sign in region II, so t becomes spacelike and r timelike there; regions I and III are static, II is not.

sections.title: Space-time diagram of the Reissner-Nordström solution
sections.summary: Restricting to epsilon^2 < m^2, defines a new time tbar that straightens ingoing radial light rays and brings the metric to a form regular for all r > 0. Radial null rays split into an ingoing family tbar + r = constant and an outgoing family with slope (1+f)/(1-f). Instead of integrating, the authors read that slope from graphs of 1+f and 1-f (Fig. 19.3) and assemble the spacetime diagram of Fig. 19.4: cones tip over at r_plus, which is therefore an event horizon; in region II all cones point to smaller r; in region III the cones straighten again so infall to the singularity is not compulsory.
key_moves: Choose tbar = t + h(r) with h' = f/(1-f), giving the logarithmic expression (19.17) valid for r > r_plus.
The metric (19.18) with f = 2m/r - epsilon^2/r^2 (19.19) has no zero denominators, so it covers r_plus and r_minus.
Radial null condition (19.20) yields ingoing lines tbar + r = const (19.21) and outgoing slope (19.22).

Slope tour: 45 degrees at infinity, steepening to vertical at r_plus, negative throughout II (least steep at r = epsilon^2/m), vertical again at r_minus, then in III falling from +infinity through 1 and 0 to -1 at r = 0.
Light cones at r_plus show no signal can leave II for I: r = r_plus is an event horizon.
In III the future cone again contains directions of increasing r, previewing that falling into r = 0 is avoidable.

sections.title: Neutral particles in Reissner-Nordström space-time
sections.summary: Studies radial timelike geodesics. Time-independence of the metric gives the constant u_0, and the radial equation becomes rdot^2 = u_0^2 - g_00. Plotting g_00 against r with horizontal lines at height u_0^2 (Fig. 19.5) shows that motion is confined to where the line lies above the curve: for u_0^2 < 1 the particle is trapped between a point in region I and a point in region III, for u_0^2 > 1 it comes from and returns to large r but has a minimum radius inside r_minus. The charge thus creates a repulsive barrier. Because r_minus is reached in finite proper time even though Fig. 19.4 shows only an asymptotic approach, the chart is incomplete and needs Kruskal-style extension.
concepts: gravitational repulsion near a charged mass
finite proper time versus coordinate asymptotics
key_moves: Radial timelike conditions (19.23) with proper time as parameter; covariant 4-velocity introduced.
The t-component of the geodesic equation integrates to u_0 = constant (19.24).
The normalization condition becomes rdot^2 = A with A = u_0^2 - g_00 (19.25-19.26).
Turning points where the energy line meets g_00; allowed region wherever u_0^2 >= g_00.
Bounded case u_0^2 < 1 between r_Q (III) and r_P (I); unbounded case u_0^2 > 1 with closest approach r_R in III.
Finite proper time to r_minus versus asymptotic approach in the diagram is read as a sign that the manifold is not maximal.

sections.title: Penrose diagrams of the maximal analytic extensions
sections.summary: Builds the Kruskal analogue for epsilon^2 < m^2: a tortoise coordinate r*, double null coordinates v, w that put the radial part of the metric in the form g_00 dv dw, and exponentials v', w' whose rate is tuned so the metric is regular across r_plus. Compactifying with arctan gives the Penrose diagram of Fig. 19.6.
key_moves: Define v = t + r*, w = t - r* in region I with r* from (19.28) (19.27).
Metric becomes (1 - 2m/r + epsilon^2/r^2) dv dw plus the sphere part, with r(v, w) implicit (19.29).
Exponentiate with rate (r_plus - r_minus)/(2 r_plus^2) (19.30) so that the zero of g_00 at r_plus is cancelled (19.31); r(v', w') is implicit (19.32).
Apply arctan to each null coordinate (19.33) to draw the Penrose diagram.
The chart (19.31) is still singular at r_minus; infinitely many further null charts are needed to patch the full manifold.

sections.title: Global structure and physics of the extended spacetime (within §19.5)
sections.summary: Interprets Fig. 19.6 and closes the chapter. The extension contains an unending vertical sequence of asymptotically flat exteriors joined by regions II and III; the r = 0 singularity is timelike and can be dodged, so a timelike worldline can pass I -> II -> III -> II -> a new I, a speculative one-way 'wormhole' trip unless exterior regions are identified. It notes infinite redshift of infalling matter as seen from region I, trapped spheres in region II, and the startling fact that an observer crossing r_minus receives the entire future of their exterior in finite proper time, implying infinite blueshift and probable instability. The extremal (epsilon^2 = m^2) and super-extremal (epsilon^2 > m^2) Penrose diagrams are shown in Figs. 19.7 and 19.8 without derivation.
concepts: infinite redshift at the event horizon
infinite blueshift at the inner horizon
key_moves: Count regions: infinitely many I's, joined by II and III blocks; singularities appear as vertical (timelike) wavy lines.
Exhibit a future-directed timelike curve that avoids r = 0 and exits into a different exterior.
Discuss identification of exterior regions as a way to re-emerge, noting the result depends on how it is done.
Crossing r_minus: all of the exterior's future is compressed into a finite stretch of the observer's proper time, hence blueshift and suspected instability.
Extremal case: horizons merge at r = m, region II vanishes, chain of I and III blocks (Fig. 19.7); super-extremal case: no horizon, single triangle with a naked timelike singularity (Fig. 19.8).

concepts.name: Reissner-Nordström solution
concepts.definition: The exact static, spherically symmetric, asymptotically flat solution of the Einstein-Maxwell equations for a non-rotating body of mass m and charge epsilon: g_00 = 1 - 2m/r + epsilon^2/r^2 = -1/g_11, with angular part r^2 dOmega^2 and a radial electric field that approaches epsilon/r^2. It reduces to Schwarzschild when epsilon = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated as a gentler preview of Kerr's global structure. Obtained componentwise: symmetry ansatz for metric and field, Maxwell equations first, then the Einstein equations as ODEs in r, with integration constants fixed by the Coulomb and Schwarzschild limits.
concepts.notes: Book labels the charge epsilon; many other texts use Q or e. Geometrized Gaussian units, so epsilon is a length.

concepts.name: Einstein-Maxwell field equations
concepts.definition: The coupled system in which the energy-momentum tensor of an electromagnetic field sources curvature through G_ab = 8 pi T_ab, while the field itself obeys the source-free Maxwell equations written with the covariant derivative of the curved metric.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated at the outset as the equations to solve; the Maxwell stress tensor is taken from ch12 eq (12.57).

concepts.name: trace-free Maxwell energy-momentum tensor
aliases: vanishing trace of the electromagnetic stress tensor
concepts.definition: In four dimensions the electromagnetic energy-momentum tensor satisfies T^a_a = 0; tracing the field equations then gives R = 0, so in source-free electrovac regions G_ab = 8 pi T_ab is equivalent to R_ab = 8 pi T_ab.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Exercise 13.3 and used as a labour-saving switch from the Einstein tensor to the Ricci tensor (verification is Exercise 19.1).
concepts.notes: For RN the mixed components (not printed) are T^a_b = (epsilon^2/8 pi r^4) diag(1, 1, -1, -1) in (t, r, theta, phi): positive energy density, radial tension, tangential pressure.

concepts.name: Maxwell's equations in curved spacetime
concepts.definition: The source-free field equations nabla_b F^ab = 0 and partial_[a F_bc] = 0; the second may use partial derivatives because the symmetric connection terms cancel under antisymmetrization, and the first can be evaluated as a divergence using the metric determinant.
concepts.how_introduced: Written alongside the Einstein equations; with the ansatz, the cyclic identity holds automatically and the divergence reduces to one ODE (Exercise 19.3, hinted to use ch07 eq 7.10).

concepts.name: radial electrostatic field ansatz
concepts.definition: For a charge at rest at the centre of a static spherical configuration, the only nonzero Maxwell components are F_10 = -F_01 = E(r): no magnetic field and an electric field pointing along r whose magnitude depends only on r.
concepts.how_introduced: Justified by the picture of radial field lines (Fig. 19.1) and by transforming the Cartesian Maxwell tensor to polar coordinates (Exercise 19.2).

concepts.name: static spherically symmetric line element
aliases: canonical form of the spherically symmetric metric
concepts.definition: Coordinates t, r, theta, phi in which a spherically symmetric metric reads e^nu dt^2 - e^lambda dr^2 - r^2 dOmega^2, with r the areal radius; staticity removes any t-dependence of nu and lambda.
concepts.how_introduced: Imported from ch15 eq (15.37) and immediately specialized to nu(r), lambda(r).

concepts.name: asymptotic flatness
concepts.definition: The requirement that the metric approach the Minkowski form far from the source; here nu and lambda both tend to zero as r grows without bound.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as the boundary condition that selects lambda = -nu and makes the field Coulombic at large r.

concepts.name: charge parameter of Reissner-Nordström
aliases: electric charge of the black hole
concepts.definition: The constant epsilon appearing in E = e^{(nu+lambda)/2} epsilon/r^2; it is the total charge because the field becomes the Coulomb field epsilon/r^2 at large r. In the book's geometrized Gaussian units it has the dimension of length (in SI, epsilon = Q sqrt(G/(4 pi epsilon_0))/c^2).
concepts.how_introduced: Appears as an integration constant of the Maxwell equation and is named by comparison with the classical point-charge field.
concepts.notes: The SI conversion is our addition; the book does not discuss units for epsilon in this chapter.

concepts.name: geometric mass
concepts.definition: The length m = GM/c^2 that multiplies 1/r in g_00; in RN it is identified as the mass because the solution becomes Schwarzschild when the charge vanishes.
concepts.how_introduced: Arises as the second integration constant from (r e^nu)' = 1 - epsilon^2/r^2.

concepts.name: Birkhoff theorem for Einstein-Maxwell
concepts.definition: Any spherically symmetric solution of the Einstein-Maxwell equations outside the sources is necessarily static; the book adds that asymptotic flatness is likewise forced, so neither assumption used in the derivation restricts the result, which is always Reissner-Nordström.
concepts.how_introduced: After the derivation the authors remark that staticity and asymptotic flatness were not really needed, exactly as for Schwarzschild, skip the longer general calculation, and put the staticity statement in a shaded theorem box as the charged counterpart of Birkhoff's theorem.

concepts.name: intrinsic singularity
concepts.definition: A location where a scalar built from curvature diverges, so no change of coordinates can make the geometry regular there; r = 0 in RN.
concepts.how_introduced: Asserted for r = 0 by pointing to the divergence of the Riemann invariant R^abcd R_abcd.

concepts.name: coordinate singularity
concepts.definition: A breakdown of metric components caused by the chart rather than the geometry: curvature invariants stay finite and a better coordinate system is regular there; r = r_plus and r = r_minus in RN.
concepts.how_introduced: Shown by the failure of (19.14) at the roots of Q and removed by the Eddington-Finkelstein-type chart (19.18).

concepts.name: Kretschmann scalar
concepts.definition: The full contraction R^abcd R_abcd of the Riemann tensor, a coordinate-invariant scalar whose divergence certifies a genuine curvature singularity.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in passing as the test that r = 0 is intrinsic; not computed.
concepts.notes: Explicit value is the standard result, not printed in the book.

concepts.name: horizon radii r_plus and r_minus
concepts.definition: The positive roots r_plus/minus = m +/- sqrt(m^2 - epsilon^2) of Q(r) = r^2 - 2mr + epsilon^2, where g_00 vanishes; they satisfy r_plus + r_minus = 2m and r_plus r_minus = epsilon^2. The outer one is the event horizon, the inner one a second null surface inside the hole.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by writing g_00 = Q/r^2 and solving the quadratic; displayed on the graph of g_00 (Fig. 19.2).

concepts.name: sub-extremal, extremal and super-extremal classification
concepts.definition: Sorting RN spacetimes by Delta = m^2 - epsilon^2: two distinct horizons when positive, a single degenerate horizon at r = m when zero (region II absent), and no horizon at all when negative.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced through the discriminant of Q in §19.2, then carried to the end, where each case gets its own Penrose diagram (Figs. 19.6-19.8).
concepts.notes: Book does not use the words extremal or sub-extremal; it names the cases by the inequality.

concepts.name: naked singularity
concepts.definition: A curvature singularity not hidden behind any event horizon, so signals from it can reach distant observers; RN with epsilon^2 > m^2 has one at r = 0, and the spacetime is already inextendible.
concepts.how_introduced: Only shown pictorially: Fig. 19.8 is a single triangle whose left edge is the timelike singularity.
concepts.notes: The term 'naked singularity' is ours; the book says the case is inextendible.

concepts.name: interchange of timelike and spacelike coordinate character
concepts.definition: Where g_00 < 0 (between the horizons) the coordinate t labels a spacelike direction and r a timelike one, so constant-r observers cannot exist and the region is not static; decreasing r becomes as unavoidable as advancing time.
concepts.how_introduced: Read from the sign of g_00 in Fig. 19.2 and stated as a direct echo of the Schwarzschild interior.

concepts.name: advanced Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates
concepts.definition: A new time tbar = t + h(r), with h' = f/(1-f), chosen so ingoing radial light rays satisfy tbar + r = constant; the resulting line element has no divergent coefficients at the horizons and covers all r > 0 in one chart.
concepts.how_introduced: Constructed by analogy with ch17: find the ingoing null congruence, then absorb its logarithms into the time coordinate (Exercise 19.10); piecewise versions for regions II and III and for the other charge cases are exercises 19.11-19.12. The retarded (outgoing) counterpart is Exercise 19.7.

concepts.name: radial null geodesic congruences
concepts.definition: The two families of radial light rays through each event: in the tbar chart the ingoing family is a set of straight lines tbar + r = constant and the other family obeys dtbar/dr = (1+f)/(1-f).
concepts.how_introduced: Derived from the null condition with fixed angles (19.20); the 'outgoing' family keeps its name even where it moves to smaller r.

concepts.name: light-cone slope analysis
concepts.definition: Drawing a spacetime diagram without solving for null curves: evaluate the slope of each ray family as a function of position, from plotted auxiliary functions, and place light cones accordingly.
concepts.how_introduced: Used for the outgoing family, whose slope is read off the mirror-image graphs of 1+f and 1-f (Fig. 19.3) to produce Fig. 19.4.
concepts.notes: The three landmark radii are our explicit values for the slope tour described in words.

concepts.name: event horizon
concepts.definition: The boundary of the set of events that can send signals to distant observers; for RN it is the null surface r = r_plus, through which light cones tip so that nothing inside can return to region I.
concepts.how_introduced: Identified from the light cones drawn at r_plus in the Eddington-Finkelstein-type diagram, echoing ch17.

concepts.name: inner (Cauchy) horizon
concepts.definition: The null surface r = r_minus inside a sub-extremal RN hole. Beyond it the future is no longer fixed by data given in the exterior; an observer crossing it receives the entire future history of their exterior region in finite proper time, so incoming radiation is infinitely blueshifted.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears first as the second root of Q, then as a place Fig. 19.4 seems never to be crossed, and finally in the Penrose diagram, where its blueshift property and suspected instability are discussed.
concepts.notes: The book does not use the term Cauchy horizon.

concepts.name: timelike singularity
concepts.definition: A singularity whose locus is timelike, drawn as a vertical line in a Penrose diagram; future-directed timelike curves are not forced into it and can pass by, unlike the spacelike Schwarzschild singularity.
concepts.how_introduced: Anticipated by the upright light cones of region III, then made explicit in the Penrose diagram, with a worldline that avoids it.

concepts.name: conserved energy of radial geodesics
concepts.definition: Because the metric does not depend on t, the covariant time component u_0 = g_00 dt/dtau of a geodesic's 4-velocity is constant; it is the particle's energy per unit rest mass as judged at infinity, with u_0^2 < 1 for bound and > 1 for unbound motion.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained as a first integral of the geodesic equations for radial motion (Exercise 19.15).

concepts.name: effective potential for radial motion
concepts.definition: Writing the radial equation as rdot^2 = u_0^2 - g_00, so g_00(r) plays the role of a potential and u_0^2 of an energy: motion is allowed where u_0^2 >= g_00 and turns around where they are equal.
concepts.how_introduced: Built on the same g_00 graph as Fig. 19.2, now with horizontal lines at height u_0^2 marking turning points P, Q, R (Fig. 19.5).

concepts.name: gravitational repulsion near a charged mass
concepts.definition: Because g_00 grows without bound as r -> 0 when epsilon is nonzero, every radial neutral geodesic has a minimum radius inside r_minus and is turned back; neutral test particles cannot reach the singularity on radial paths.
concepts.how_introduced: Read from Fig. 19.5; the book frames it as a potential barrier produced by the point charge.
concepts.notes: The mass-function reading (field energy outside radius r is subtracted, making the enclosed mass negative for r < epsilon^2/2m) is our gloss, not in the text.

concepts.name: finite proper time versus coordinate asymptotics
concepts.definition: A worldline may appear to approach a surface only asymptotically in some coordinates and yet reach it after finite proper time; this means the coordinates stop covering the manifold there and an extension is needed.
concepts.how_introduced: Applied to a particle approaching r_minus in Fig. 19.4, compared explicitly with the Schwarzschild-coordinate infall diagram Fig. 17.7.

concepts.name: maximal analytic extension
concepts.definition: A spacetime extended by analytic continuation of the metric until no further extension is possible, so every geodesic either runs to infinite affine parameter or ends on a genuine singularity.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the finite-proper-time argument and carried out for epsilon^2 < m^2 following the Kruskal construction of §18.2; stated to be trivial (inextendible) for epsilon^2 > m^2.
prerequisites: finite proper time versus coordinate asymptotics

concepts.name: tortoise coordinate
concepts.definition: A radial function with dr*/dr = 1/g_00, which sends r_plus to r* = -infinity; along radial light rays t +/- r* is constant.
concepts.how_introduced: Written down for r > r_plus as the ingredient of the double null coordinates; it coincides with the r-dependent part of tbar plus r.

concepts.name: double null coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates v = t + r*, w = t - r* that are constant along outgoing and ingoing radial light rays respectively, making the radial-temporal part of the metric proportional to dv dw.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced in region I as the first step of the Kruskal recipe (Exercise 19.16).

concepts.name: Kruskal-type coordinates
concepts.definition: Null coordinates v' = exp(kappa v), w' = -exp(-kappa w) with kappa = (r_plus - r_minus)/(2 r_plus^2); the exponential rate is fixed so the factor (r - r_plus) in g_00 cancels, leaving a metric regular across r = r_plus but still degenerate at r_minus.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the charged analogue of the Kruskal transformation, with r(v', w') defined implicitly.
concepts.notes: A second family of such charts (the book says infinitely many) is needed to cross r_minus; not carried out.

concepts.name: surface gravity
concepts.definition: For a static horizon, the constant kappa that sets the exponential relation between Kruskal-type and static null coordinates (and the exponential redshift of signals from near the horizon); for the RN outer horizon kappa = (r_plus - r_minus)/(2 r_plus^2), reducing to 1/4m for Schwarzschild and vanishing in the extremal case.
concepts.how_introduced: Not named: it appears only as the unexplained rate constant inside the exponentials of (19.30).
concepts.notes: Naming and interpretation are ours; useful for explaining why the extremal case needs different coordinates.

concepts.name: Penrose diagram
concepts.definition: A picture of the radial-temporal geometry after a conformal rescaling that brings infinity to finite distance (here via arctan of the null coordinates), keeping radial light rays at 45 degrees so causal structure can be read by eye.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained from the Kruskal-type chart by (19.33) and drawn for all three charge cases, with static-coordinate grids overlaid on selected blocks.

concepts.name: conformal infinity
concepts.definition: Boundary labels of a Penrose diagram: future and past timelike infinity i^+ and i^-, spatial infinity i^0, and future and past null infinity scri^+ and scri^- where outgoing and incoming light rays end and begin.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as labels on every asymptotic region of Figs. 19.6-19.8, carried over from ch18.

concepts.name: multiple asymptotically flat universes
concepts.definition: The maximally extended sub-extremal RN spacetime contains infinitely many separate exterior regions I, stacked in time and linked by regions II and III; a timelike traveller can go from one exterior into a later one but not back.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off the Penrose diagram of Fig. 19.6 with an explicit worldline from P; linked to the speculative idea of charge-produced wormholes.

concepts.name: identification of asymptotic regions
concepts.definition: Declaring distinct copies of region I in the extension to be the same physical region, which changes the global topology and lets a traveller re-emerge from the hole into their own universe, with the destination depending on how the identification is chosen.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as a possible way around the one-way nature of the journey.

concepts.name: infinite redshift at the event horizon
concepts.definition: Signals sent by an object as it crosses r_plus reach observers who stay in region I with a redshift that grows without bound; in static coordinates the surfaces g_00 = 0 are surfaces of infinite redshift.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated briefly in the discussion of Fig. 19.6; Exercise 19.6 asks for these surfaces.

concepts.name: trapped surface
concepts.definition: A closed spacelike 2-surface for which both families of future-directed null normals converge, so even outward light loses area; every symmetry sphere in region II of RN is trapped.
concepts.how_introduced: Asserted in one sentence about region II without a formal definition in this chapter.
prerequisites: interchange of timelike and spacelike coordinate character

concepts.name: infinite blueshift at the inner horizon
concepts.definition: Because an observer crossing r_minus intercepts light from the entire infinite future of region I in a finite proper time, radiation falling in is blueshifted without bound there, which suggests that small perturbations would destroy the smooth inner horizon.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as a bizarre property of the extension and a topic then under research; Exercise 19.17 asks the reader to verify it from Fig. 19.6.
concepts.notes: Later literature (mass inflation, strong cosmic censorship) developed this; the book does not follow it up.

concepts.name: Kerr solution
concepts.definition: The stationary, axisymmetric vacuum solution describing a rotating black hole, which shares with RN two horizons, a timelike singularity and an infinite chain of regions in its maximal extension.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in the opening sentence as the reason RN deserves study; developed in ch20.

key_equations.name: Einstein-Maxwell field equations
key_equations.meaning: Curvature is sourced by the Maxwell energy-momentum tensor (geometrized units, no cosmological term).
key_equations.symbols: G_ab Einstein tensor; T_ab electromagnetic energy-momentum tensor from (12.57)

key_equations.name: Ricci form for trace-free sources
key_equations.meaning: Equivalent form valid because T^a_a = 0 forces R = 0.

key_equations.name: Inhomogeneous Maxwell equation, source-free
key_equations.meaning: The field has no sources outside the point charge.
key_equations.symbols: F^ab Maxwell tensor; nabla covariant derivative

key_equations.name: Homogeneous Maxwell equation
key_equations.meaning: Cyclic identity; satisfied automatically by the radial ansatz.

key_equations.name: Canonical spherically symmetric line element
key_equations.meaning: General spherical metric with two unknown functions.
key_equations.symbols: nu, lambda functions of t and r (then of r only)

key_equations.name: Static condition
key_equations.meaning: Staticity removes time dependence.

key_equations.name: Radial field ansatz
key_equations.meaning: Only the t-r components of the field are nonzero, representing a radial electric field.
key_equations.symbols: E(r) field strength function; rows/columns ordered t, r, theta, phi

key_equations.name: Reduced Maxwell equation
key_equations.meaning: The divergence of F^ab collapses to conservation of a flux-like quantity through spheres.

key_equations.name: Electric field solution
key_equations.meaning: Integrates (19.8); with lambda = -nu it becomes exactly epsilon/r^2.

key_equations.name: Asymptotic flatness
key_equations.meaning: Boundary condition fixing constants.

key_equations.name: Combined 00 and 11 field equations
key_equations.meaning: Gives lambda = -nu, so g_00 g_11 = -1 as in Schwarzschild.

key_equations.name: Angular field equation
key_equations.meaning: The one remaining independent equation; the charge term is the field-energy correction.

key_equations.name: Metric function
key_equations.meaning: Integral of (19.12) with a second constant m.

key_equations.name: Reissner-Nordström line element
key_equations.meaning: The exterior geometry of a static charged mass; Schwarzschild when epsilon = 0.
key_equations.symbols: m mass, epsilon charge, both lengths

key_equations.name: RN mixed energy-momentum tensor (not printed)
key_equations.meaning: Energy density of the Coulomb field, radial tension equal to it, tangential pressure equal to it; traceless. Our computation to support Exercise 19.4.

key_equations.name: Metric coefficients via Q
key_equations.meaning: Reduces the horizon question to the zeros of a quadratic.

key_equations.name: The quadratic Q
key_equations.meaning: Numerator of g_00.

key_equations.name: Discriminant
key_equations.meaning: Sign selects zero, one or two horizons. Note: unlike Kerr-literature Delta = r^2 - 2mr + a^2, this Delta is a constant.

key_equations.name: Horizon radii
key_equations.meaning: Outer (event) and inner horizon radii where g_00 vanishes.

key_equations.name: Vieta relations (our addition)
key_equations.meaning: Handy for checking (19.17), (19.28) and (19.31); shows epsilon^2/m is the harmonic mean of the horizon radii.

key_equations.name: Advanced Eddington-Finkelstein-type time (r > r_+)
key_equations.meaning: Time shift whose r-derivative is f/(1-f) = (2mr - epsilon^2)/Q, straightening ingoing light rays.

key_equations.name: RN metric in Eddington-Finkelstein-type form
key_equations.meaning: Regular for all r > 0; one chart covering regions I, II, III.

key_equations.name: Definition of f
key_equations.meaning: Deviation of g_00 from flat.

key_equations.name: Radial null conditions
key_equations.meaning: Light rays moving radially.

key_equations.name: Ingoing null rays
key_equations.meaning: Straight lines at -45 degrees in the (r, tbar) diagram.

key_equations.name: Outgoing null ray slope
key_equations.meaning: Slope of the second null family; infinite where f = 1 (horizons), 1 where f = 0, 0 where f = -1, tending to -1 at r = 0.

key_equations.name: Slope landmarks (our explicit values)
key_equations.meaning: Radii at which the described slope tour turns: least steep point in region II, slope 1 and slope 0 in region III (Exercise 19.14).

key_equations.name: Radial timelike geodesic conditions
key_equations.meaning: Radial motion parametrized by proper time with unit 4-velocity norm.

key_equations.name: Energy first integral
key_equations.meaning: Conserved covariant time component of 4-velocity (energy per unit mass).

key_equations.name: Radial equation
key_equations.meaning: Energy-type equation for r(tau).

key_equations.name: Effective potential form
key_equations.meaning: g_00 acts as the potential; motion requires u_0^2 >= g_00.

key_equations.name: Double null coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Coordinates constant along radial light rays in region I.

key_equations.name: Tortoise coordinate
key_equations.meaning: Solves dr*/dr = 1/g_00 for r > r_+.

key_equations.name: Double null form
key_equations.meaning: Radial part conformally flat; r(v, w) implicit via (v - w)/2 = r*.

key_equations.name: Kruskal-type null coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Exponential map with rate kappa = (r_+ - r_-)/(2 r_+^2) chosen to regularize r = r_+.

key_equations.name: Kruskal-type RN metric
key_equations.meaning: Regular across r = r_+; the conformal factor vanishes at r = r_-, where this chart fails.

key_equations.name: Implicit r(v', w') as printed
key_equations.meaning: Relation defining r in the Kruskal-type chart. As printed, every exponent is half the value implied by (19.28) and (19.30); the self-consistent version (which also reproduces (19.31)) is given in the next entry.

key_equations.name: Implicit r(v', w') corrected (our check)
key_equations.meaning: Follows from v'w' = -exp(kappa(v - w)) with v - w = 2r*; verified numerically to be the relation for which (19.31) holds.

key_equations.name: Conformal compactification
key_equations.meaning: Maps the infinite Kruskal-type plane to a finite region for the Penrose diagram.

key_equations.name: Surface gravity of the outer horizon (our naming)
key_equations.meaning: The rate constant in (19.30); tends to 1/4m when epsilon = 0 and to 0 in the extremal limit.

key_equations.name: Exercise 19.11 transformations for regions II and III
key_equations.meaning: Same derivative as (19.17), with log arguments made positive in each band. Recovered from the page render; the text export garbles the first form.

key_equations.name: Exercise 19.12 transformations, extremal and super-extremal (sign corrected)
key_equations.meaning: Coordinates bringing (19.14) to (19.18) in the other two cases. The book prints r^2 - 2mr - epsilon^2 inside the logarithm; the plus sign is required for the derivative to equal (2mr - epsilon^2)/Q.

figures.label: Fig. 19.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: Electric field lines of a point charge point straight outward.
figures.visual_description: Two concentric circles around a central dot labelled O. Short arrows point radially outward, about six starting on the inner circle and about seven on the outer circle, placed at irregular angles so they do not line up between circles. No axes or numbers.
figures.what_it_teaches: The field of a static point charge has only a radial component depending on r, which is why F_ab reduces to a single function E(r) in the t-r block.

redesign.idea: Flux shells: nested spheres around a charge with field arrows whose length follows E(r); a readout multiplies |E| by the area of the sphere in the RN geometry to show the conserved flux behind (19.8).
redesign.interaction: Learner drags a probe sphere radius and toggles between flat space and RN (sliders for m, epsilon); arrow lengths and the flux counter update, showing flux stays epsilon while E follows epsilon/r^2 because the areal radius is used.

figures.label: Fig. 19.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: The time-time metric coefficient against radius for a charged and an uncharged hole.
figures.visual_description: Horizontal r-axis starting at a vertical axis marked r = 0, with a horizontal guide line at height 1. A solid curve labelled g_00 plunges from very large values near r = 0, crosses the axis at a tick r_-, dips to a single minimum below the axis, climbs back through the axis at r_+ and approaches 1 from below at large r. A dashed curve labelled with subscript S g_00 rises from far below near the origin, crosses the axis at 2m (to the right of r_+), and approaches 1 from below, staying under the solid curve everywhere.
figures.what_it_teaches: Charge turns the Schwarzschild divergence to minus infinity at small r into a divergence to plus infinity, creating a second zero (r_-), pulling the outer zero inside 2m, and leaving a band where g_00 < 0 in which t and r swap roles.
concepts: interchange of timelike and spacelike coordinate character

redesign.idea: Charge dial: a live plot of g_00(r) for RN with the Schwarzschild curve as a ghost, shaded red where g_00 < 0 (non-static band) and with markers at r_-, r_+ and 2m.
redesign.interaction: Learner moves an epsilon/m slider from 0 past 1; the two roots slide together, merge at r = m, then disappear, and a badge flips between 'two horizons', 'extremal', and 'naked singularity'. Hovering a radius shows whether t is timelike there.

figures.label: Fig. 19.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Plots of 1 + f and 1 - f against radius.
figures.visual_description: r-axis with ticks r_- and r_+ and a horizontal guide line at height 1. The curve labelled 1 + f rises steeply from below at small r, crosses the guide line where it meets the other curve, climbs to a broad hump roughly midway between r_- and r_+, then decays to 1 from above. The curve labelled 1 - f is its mirror image in the guide line: falling from high values at small r, crossing the axis at r_-, dipping to a trough below the axis between r_- and r_+, rising through the axis at r_+ and approaching 1 from below.
figures.what_it_teaches: The ratio of these two curves is the slope of the outgoing null rays, so one can see where the slope is infinite (zeros of 1 - f), equal to 1 (crossing), zero (zero of 1 + f) and negative, without integrating anything.

redesign.idea: Linked slope reader: the two curves on top, a single light cone below that is redrawn with edges of slope -1 and (1+f)/(1-f) at the probe radius.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags a vertical probe across r; the cone tilts, flips through vertical at r_+ and r_-, and the numeric slope is shown; checkpoints at r = epsilon^2/m, epsilon^2/2m and the zero of 1+f light up as they are passed.

figures.label: Fig. 19.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: Spacetime diagram of a sub-extremal charged hole in advanced Eddington-Finkelstein-type coordinates.
figures.visual_description: Vertical tbar axis drawn as a wavy line labelled Singularity r = 0, horizontal r axis. Vertical lines mark r = r_- and r = r_+, splitting the plane into regions III (left), II (middle), I (right). A family of parallel straight lines slopes down to the right at 45 degrees across all regions (ingoing rays). Curved outgoing rays: in I they rise to the right, flattening toward 45 degrees far out and hugging the r_+ line toward the past; in II they are S-shaped curves running from near r_+ at the bottom up and leftward toward r_-; in III they are U-shaped, rising steeply along r_- on the right and at 45 degrees toward the singularity on the left with a lowest point between. Small ellipse-shaped light cones sit at intersections of the two families, tipped to point inward in II and upright in III and I.
figures.what_it_teaches: r_+ is an event horizon because cones there cannot point back into I; in II every future direction decreases r; in III cones no longer force motion toward r = 0, so the singularity is avoidable; in these coordinates outgoing rays in III only approach r_- asymptotically, hinting at incompleteness.

redesign.idea: Numerically integrated Eddington-Finkelstein diagram with a field of light cones, plus a 'launch' tool for photons and massive particles.
redesign.interaction: Learner sets m and epsilon, clicks an event to fire inward/outward photons or a radial geodesic with chosen energy; rays are integrated live, cones are drawn along the path, and a proper-time counter shows the particle reaching r_- in finite tau even though the ray appears to crawl along it.

figures.caption_paraphrase: Uncaptioned decorative element: a blank ruled note grid in the page margin.
figures.visual_description: A tall, narrow grid of empty rectangular cells, two columns wide and roughly two dozen rows high, printed in the left margin beside the start of §19.4. It has no labels, curves or text.
figures.what_it_teaches: Nothing about physics; it is a note-taking design element of this edition.

figures.label: Fig. 19.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: Energy lines on the g_00 curve show confined and escaping radial motion of an uncharged particle.
figures.visual_description: The g_00 curve against r, with a horizontal guide at height 1 and vertical lines at r_- and r_+ dividing the plot into regions III, II, I (labels sit just above the height-1 guide). A dashed horizontal line below 1 meets the curve at Q on the steep left branch (inside r_-) and at P on the right branch (outside r_+). A dotted horizontal line above 1 meets the steep left branch at R. Ticks on the r-axis mark r_R and r_Q (left of r_-) and r_P (right of r_+). The curve dips to a minimum below the axis in region II.
figures.what_it_teaches: With g_00 as a potential, an energy below 1 gives motion confined between r_Q and r_P, an energy above 1 gives motion that comes in from infinity and turns back at r_R; either way the particle cannot reach r = 0, because the charge term makes a barrier.
concepts: gravitational repulsion near a charged mass

redesign.idea: Energy-line playground: draggable horizontal energy line over g_00, an animated bead moving in r with speed sqrt(u_0^2 - g_00), and a linked Penrose-diagram panel tracing the same worldline.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags u_0^2 and the charge slider; turning points update, the bead oscillates or escapes, and the Penrose panel shows that each 'bounce' actually carries the particle into a new region I rather than back home.

figures.label: Fig. 19.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: Penrose diagram of the maximally extended sub-extremal charged black hole.
figures.visual_description: A vertically repeating tiling drawn with dashed horizon lines and wavy vertical singularities. At two levels a pair of diamond exteriors I sits left and right, each with corners i^+, i^0, i^- and outer edges scri^+ and scri^- (r = infinity) and inner edges r = r_+. Above each pair a square region II (between r_+ and r_- dashed lines) leads up to two regions III, each bounded on its outer side by a vertical wavy line marked Singularity r = 0; above them a further region II opens into the next pair of exteriors, and the pattern runs off the top and bottom. Coordinate grids are drawn only in the lower part: the lower-left exterior I and the past region II diamond wedged below and between the lower pair of exteriors are densely filled with t = constant lines fanning from corners and r = constant curves (pointer labels on both sides), and a partial r = constant grid fills the bottom region III beside the lower-left singularity. The lower-right exterior carries no grid; instead a curved arrow starts at a point P there, climbs through II, the right-hand III and the next II, and ends inside the upper-right exterior I.
figures.what_it_teaches: The extension contains infinitely many exterior universes; the singularities are timelike and avoidable; a traveller can pass through the hole into a different exterior but cannot come back; r_- is where an observer receives the whole future of the exterior they left.

redesign.idea: Scrollable infinite Penrose ladder with a worldline editor and signal tracer.
redesign.interaction: Learner sketches a timelike worldline (the app enforces the 45-degree cone constraint) from a region I; blocks highlight as they are entered; a 'send light from exterior' button fires rays from successive exterior times toward the traveller, and a blueshift meter spikes as the worldline nears r_-. Toggle overlays t = const and r = const grids, and an 'identify exteriors' switch glues regions I to show the topology change.

figures.label: Fig. 19.8
figures.caption_paraphrase: Penrose diagram when the charge exceeds the mass.
figures.visual_description: A single triangle. Its left edge is a vertical wavy line from i^- at the bottom to i^+ at the top, labelled Singularity r = 0. The two right edges, scri^+ (upper) and scri^- (lower), meet at i^0 on the right. Several arcs curve from i^- to i^+, bowing toward i^0, with a pointer label r = constant. No horizons or dashed lines.
figures.what_it_teaches: With epsilon^2 > m^2 nothing hides the singularity: the spacetime is like Minkowski's half-diagram with a timelike singular boundary that can send signals to infinity; no extension is needed.

redesign.idea: Morphing Penrose diagram shared with Fig. 19.6 and 19.7: as epsilon/m passes 1 the chain of blocks collapses into this single triangle.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags epsilon/m; the app animates the horizons merging and vanishing and lets the learner shoot light from the singularity to scri^+ to see it is visible.

figures.label: Fig. 19.7
figures.caption_paraphrase: Penrose diagram of the extremal charged black hole.
figures.visual_description: A vertical wavy line on the left labelled Singularity r = 0 runs the whole height. To its right a column alternates between triangular regions III (touching the singularity, bounded by dashed lines r = m) and diamond regions I whose right edges are scri^+ and scri^- labelled r = infinity. Region II is absent: I and III blocks share dashed r = m edges directly. The middle diamond I and the lower region III are filled with t = constant lines fanning from the left corner and r = constant curves, with pointer labels. The pattern continues above and below.
figures.what_it_teaches: When charge equals mass the two horizons coincide at r = m, the nonstatic band disappears, and the extended spacetime is an infinite chain of exteriors and interiors with the singularity on one side only.

redesign.idea: Middle frame of the charge-morph animation, with the degenerate horizon highlighted and a comparison inset of g_00 touching zero at r = m.
redesign.interaction: Learner scrubs epsilon/m near 1 and watches regions II shrink to zero width in the diagram while the dip of g_00 below the axis vanishes.

worked_examples.problem: Find the static, spherically symmetric, asymptotically flat solution of the Einstein-Maxwell equations produced by a point charge.
worked_examples.method: Trace argument to use R_ab; canonical metric with nu(r), lambda(r); radial F_ab; solve the divergence Maxwell equation; compute T_ab; combine the 00 and 11 components to get lambda = -nu; integrate the 22 component; fix constants by flatness at infinity, the Coulomb limit and the Schwarzschild limit.
worked_examples.key_insight: The same symmetry reduction as for Schwarzschild works; the Coulomb field contributes an energy that makes (r e^nu)' fall short of 1 by epsilon^2/r^2, which becomes the +epsilon^2/r^2 term.

worked_examples.problem: Determine where the RN metric is singular and what kind of singularity each is, for all values of charge relative to mass.
worked_examples.method: Write g_00 = Q/r^2, compute the discriminant of Q, find its roots, check the sign of g_00 in each band, and cite a curvature invariant for r = 0.
worked_examples.key_insight: Horizon structure is a property of a quadratic; the sign of g_00 tells which coordinate is timelike in each band.
worked_examples.result: No horizons if epsilon^2 > m^2; one at r = m if equal; r_plus/minus = m +/- sqrt(m^2 - epsilon^2) otherwise; r = 0 is always a curvature singularity.

worked_examples.problem: Remove the coordinate singularities at the horizons with an Eddington-Finkelstein-type time and find the radial null geodesics.
worked_examples.method: Shift t by a function of r whose derivative is f/(1-f), expand ds^2, then set angular velocities and ds^2 to zero and solve the quadratic in dtbar/dr.
worked_examples.key_insight: Choosing the shift to cancel the cross-term denominator makes the ingoing rays exactly straight, and the metric coefficients polynomial in 1/r.
worked_examples.result: Metric (19.18); ingoing rays tbar + r = const; outgoing slope (1+f)/(1-f).

worked_examples.problem: Sketch the light cones throughout regions I, II, III without solving the outgoing null equation.
worked_examples.method: Graph 1+f and 1-f, then track the sign and size of their ratio from infinity inward: 45 degrees at infinity, vertical at r_+, negative in II with an extremum at r = epsilon^2/m, vertical at r_-, then 1, 0 and finally -1 at the origin in III.
worked_examples.key_insight: Horizons are exactly where the second ray family turns vertical, and region III's cones stand upright again, so the singularity can be avoided.
worked_examples.result: Fig. 19.4 and the identification of r = r_+ as an event horizon.

worked_examples.problem: Classify the radial motion of an uncharged test particle in RN spacetime.
worked_examples.method: Use the t-independence to get u_0 constant, reduce the normalization condition to rdot^2 = u_0^2 - g_00, and read allowed ranges from horizontal lines on the g_00 graph.
worked_examples.key_insight: g_00 diverges to plus infinity at the centre, so every radial path has an inner turning point: charge makes gravity effectively repulsive at small r.
worked_examples.result: Bound motion between r_Q < r_- and r_P > r_+ if u_0^2 < 1; unbound motion with closest approach r_R < r_- if u_0^2 > 1; r = 0 never reached.
concepts: gravitational repulsion near a charged mass

worked_examples.problem: Construct coordinates regular across the outer horizon and use them to draw the Penrose diagram of the maximal extension.
worked_examples.method: Tortoise coordinate from 1/g_00; double null v, w; exponentiate with rate (r_+ - r_-)/(2 r_+^2) so the (r - r_+) factor cancels; compactify each null coordinate with arctan.
worked_examples.key_insight: The exponential rate must match the logarithmic coefficient of ln(r - r_+) in r*, which is what removes the zero of g_00; the other horizon needs its own chart.
worked_examples.result: Metric (19.31) with r(v', w') implicit, and the infinite Penrose ladder of Fig. 19.6 (note the printed exponents in (19.32) are halved).

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Energy-line diagram of one-dimensional mechanics: a horizontal energy level over a potential curve, with motion allowed only where the level lies above the curve.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: g_00 is drawn as the potential and u_0^2 as the energy; turning points P, Q, R are where the level meets the curve, making bound, unbound and repelled motion visible at a glance.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: rdot is the derivative with respect to proper time, not coordinate time; region II has g_00 < 0 so motion there is compulsory rather than 'kinetic energy'; the picture hides that the particle enters different universes on each passage.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Bead-on-a-potential animation whose bead position is mirrored by a worldline drawn in a linked Penrose diagram.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Charged hole as Schwarzschild with a second horizon: r = r_+ behaves just like r = 2m.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The authors repeatedly borrow Schwarzschild conclusions (coordinate singularity, swapped coordinate roles, disconnected-looking regions, EF and Kruskal fixes) and then isolate what the second root changes.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Beyond r_- the analogy fails: the singularity is timelike, the cones straighten, and the global structure repeats forever.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Side-by-side synchronized diagrams of Schwarzschild and RN with a slider taking epsilon from 0 upward.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Coulomb's law of a classical point charge.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The large-r behaviour epsilon/r^2 of the field is matched to the familiar Coulomb field to name epsilon as the charge.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Near the hole E is the field in the areal-radius coordinate of a curved space; the constant is in geometrized Gaussian units, not coulombs.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Tipping light cones: cones lean further inward as one approaches a horizon and topple over inside it.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Cone orientation in each region decides what is inevitable: no escape past r_+, forced inward motion in II, freedom again in III.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The tilt is coordinate dependent; only the relation of cones to r = const surfaces carries invariant meaning.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Light-cone field that smoothly re-orients as the learner drags a probe inward, with the r = const direction drawn for reference.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Wormholes produced by charges: tunnels to other universes.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The worldline in Fig. 19.6 from one exterior to another is described as a speculative trip through a charge-made wormhole, one-way unless regions are identified.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Not a traversable wormhole in the modern sense; the inner horizon is expected to be unstable, and realistic collapse does not produce the full extension.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Guided 'journey' mode in the Penrose ladder that pauses at each horizon to explain what the traveller can and cannot do.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The misleading Schwarzschild-coordinate infall picture (Fig. 17.7), where a falling particle seems never to reach r = 2m.
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: finite proper time versus coordinate asymptotics
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The apparent asymptotic approach to r_- in Fig. 19.4 is declared misleading in exactly the same way, which justifies extending the manifold.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Here the problem appears even in the improved EF-type chart, so a learner may wrongly think EF coordinates are always complete.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Mirror-image curves 1 + f and 1 - f about the line at height 1.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Plotting both makes the ratio's zeros, poles and crossings visible, turning an ODE into a graph-reading exercise.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Gives only slopes; actual ray positions and the finite-affine-parameter question require integration.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Wherever a metric component blows up there is a physical singularity, so the charged hole has singular spheres at r_+ and r_-.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only r = 0 has divergent curvature invariants; r_+ and r_- are artefacts of the static chart and disappear in Eddington-Finkelstein-type coordinates.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Metric components are what one computes first, and the formula visibly divides by zero.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Regions I, II and III are separate spacetimes because the light cones point in unrelated directions on either side of each horizon.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The disconnection is an artefact of the coordinates; the EF-type chart joins all three regions smoothly.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In static coordinates nothing seems able to cross r_plus/minus in finite coordinate time.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Once inside a black hole, everything must hit the central singularity, as for Schwarzschild.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In RN the singularity is timelike; past r_- future-directed paths can avoid it, and radial neutral particles are actually repelled before reaching it.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Schwarzschild is usually the only black hole learners have met, and 'inside a black hole' sounds like certain doom.
concepts: gravitational repulsion near a charged mass

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Because the diagram shows a particle creeping along r = r_- forever, it never crosses the inner horizon.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It reaches r_- in finite proper time; the EF-type chart is simply incomplete there, and the manifold must be extended.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The EF chart was introduced precisely to fix such problems at r_+, so learners assume it is complete.
concepts: finite proper time versus coordinate asymptotics

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Staticity and asymptotic flatness are extra assumptions without which the charged solution could be different.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: A Birkhoff-type theorem makes any spherically symmetric electrovac exterior static; the extra assumptions come for free.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: They were explicitly imposed to simplify the derivation.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A traveller who passes through a charged black hole into another universe can come back the same way.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Future-directed worldlines only move upward in the Penrose diagram, so the return is impossible unless exterior regions are identified, which changes the topology.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The word wormhole suggests a two-way tunnel.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The 'bounded' orbit between r_P and r_Q is an oscillation that keeps returning to the same exterior.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In the maximal extension each time the particle comes back out through a horizon it emerges into a new region I higher up the Penrose ladder.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Fig. 19.5 looks like an ordinary potential well with a particle rattling between walls.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The inner horizon r_- is just a second event horizon with the same character as r_+.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: r_- is where predictability from exterior data ends and where infalling radiation is infinitely blueshifted; it is expected to be unstable.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Both are roots of the same quadratic and both are null surfaces.
concepts: infinite blueshift at the inner horizon

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Charged black holes described by RN are common astrophysical objects.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Astrophysical holes are expected to be almost neutral because surrounding plasma quickly cancels any significant charge; RN is valued as a model of Kerr-like structure.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The chapter calls the epsilon^2 < m^2 case physically important and gives it full treatment.

thought_experiments.name: Trip through a charged black hole
thought_experiments.setup: An observer starts in one exterior region, falls through r_+ and r_-, swerves away from the timelike singularity and exits through another r_+ surface.
thought_experiments.lesson: The maximal extension contains other universes that can be reached but not returned from, unless one identifies exterior regions.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Pilot a spacecraft up the Penrose ladder with a thrust budget; the cone constraint is enforced and the singularity walls glow when approached.

thought_experiments.name: Watching the whole future at the inner horizon
thought_experiments.setup: An observer crosses r = r_- while signals sent from the exterior region she left, at all later exterior times, are traced forward.
thought_experiments.lesson: All those signals arrive in a finite interval of her proper time, so they are infinitely blueshifted and the inner horizon is probably unstable.
concepts: infinite blueshift at the inner horizon
thought_experiments.app_idea: Fan of light rays emitted at equal exterior time steps converging on the traveller's crossing point, with a frequency meter.

thought_experiments.name: Distant watcher of an infalling object
thought_experiments.setup: An observer who stays in region I watches a body fall through r_+.
thought_experiments.lesson: The received signals are redshifted without limit; the horizon crossing is never seen, as for Schwarzschild.
concepts: infinite redshift at the event horizon

thought_experiments.name: Dropping a neutral pebble toward a charged centre
thought_experiments.setup: A neutral particle is released or thrown radially inward with energy u_0.
thought_experiments.lesson: It crosses both horizons but is turned back at a finite minimum radius inside r_-; charge makes the centre effectively repulsive.
concepts: gravitational repulsion near a charged mass
thought_experiments.app_idea: Energy slider plus live radius-versus-proper-time plot showing the bounce.

historical_notes.event: The charged spherically symmetric solution carries their names; the chapter itself gives no history and no dates.
historical_notes.significance: First exact solution with both gravity and electromagnetism; later the prototype for black holes with inner horizons. Dates are general knowledge, not from the text.

historical_notes.event: The Large Scale Structure of Space-Time is named as the chapter's main source.
historical_notes.significance: Signals that the global-structure treatment (maximal extensions, Penrose diagrams for RN) follows the standard reference.

applications_and_observations.topic: Charge needed for an extremal solar-mass black hole (our estimate)
applications_and_observations.details: Setting geometrized charge equal to mass, epsilon = m, and converting with sqrt(4 pi epsilon_0 G) gives the charge at which horizons merge. Real holes are far below this because ambient plasma neutralizes them.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Q_extremal ~ 1.7e20 C per solar mass (sqrt(4 pi epsilon_0 G) ~ 8.6e-11 C/kg).

applications_and_observations.topic: An electron as a Reissner-Nordström object (our estimate)
applications_and_observations.details: Comparing e/m_e with the extremal ratio shows an electron would be super-extremal by an enormous factor, so a classical RN picture of it would be a naked singularity; the solution is not a model of elementary particles.
For m = 1, epsilon = 0.6 the landmarks used in the slope tour and in the Kruskal-type map can be computed directly; useful for calibrating demos.

applications_and_observations.topic: RN as a stand-in for rotating black holes
applications_and_observations.details: The book's stated reason for the chapter: the charged solution reproduces the inner structure of Kerr (two horizons, timelike singularity, repeated extension) in a spherically symmetric setting where calculations are tractable.

The authors flag the blueshift at r_- as suggesting instability and as research in progress. Subsequent theoretical work on mass inflation and strong cosmic censorship (our addition) pursued this for charged and rotating holes; it bears on whether the multi-universe extension is physical.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Signature (+, -, -, -); geometrized units with G = c = 1; field equations G_ab = 8 pi T_ab with no cosmological constant.
The black-hole charge is written epsilon (Gaussian geometrized units, dimension of length), not Q or e.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Q is reserved in this chapter for the quadratic r^2 - 2mr + epsilon^2; do not confuse with the charge Q of other books.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Q(r) = r^2 - 2mr + epsilon^2 = r^2 g_00; Delta = m^2 - epsilon^2 is a constant discriminant.
notation_and_conventions.notes: In Kerr-Newman literature Delta usually denotes the r-dependent function that this book calls Q.

notation_and_conventions.convention: g_00 = e^nu, g_11 = -e^lambda; prime means d/dr; for RN lambda = -nu.
F_ab with F_10 = E and F_01 = -E for the radial field; matrix rows/columns ordered (t, r, theta, phi).
notation_and_conventions.notes: Consistent with ch12 (12.28), where F^{0i} = E_i; lowering both indices with a (+,-,-,-) metric flips the sign, giving F_{01} = -E for a field along r.

notation_and_conventions.convention: I: r_+ < r < infinity; II: r_- < r < r_+; III: 0 < r < r_-.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Differs from the Kruskal region labels used for Schwarzschild; in the extremal case only I and III exist.

notation_and_conventions.convention: f = 1 - g_00 = 2m/r - epsilon^2/r^2; tbar is the advanced Eddington-Finkelstein-type time.
v = t + r* and w = t - r* (w, not u, for the retarded coordinate); primes for Kruskal-type versions, double primes for arctan-compactified versions.
A pre-subscript S (written S g_00) marks the Schwarzschild value 1 - 2m/r in Fig. 19.2.
u_a = g_ab dx^b/dtau; overdots are proper-time derivatives.
notation_and_conventions.notes: u_0 is the conserved energy per unit mass.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Wavy lines are curvature singularities; dashed diagonals are horizons; i^+, i^-, i^0 and script-I^+/- label infinities; bold curve families show t = const and r = const.

teaching_gems.gem: Read the causal structure off the graph of g_00 alone (Figs. 19.2 and 19.5): its zeros are the horizons and its sign says which coordinate is time in each band. A tutor can push one step further than the book: g_00 -> +infinity at the centre (RN) versus -infinity (Schwarzschild) signals a timelike versus spacelike singularity.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Compresses a whole chapter of geometry into one curve that school algebra can sketch, and makes the Schwarzschild/RN contrast visual.
teaching_gems.app_idea: g_00 plotter with a charge slider that recolours the r-axis by causal character and shows a miniature Penrose diagram updating beside it.

teaching_gems.gem: Draw light cones without solving for light rays: plot 1 + f and 1 - f and read the slope as their ratio.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Turns a differential equation into a graph-reading task and forces attention to where the slope is infinite, one, zero or negative.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Draggable probe on the two curves driving a live light cone and building the spacetime diagram cone by cone as the learner sweeps inward.

teaching_gems.gem: Reuse the same g_00 curve as the effective potential for radial geodesics, with energy as a horizontal line.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Learners already trust energy diagrams; the repulsive core then appears without any force language.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Energy-line slider with an animated particle, turning points labelled, linked to a Penrose view that shows where each bounce really goes.

teaching_gems.gem: Classify all charged black holes by the discriminant of one quadratic.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A single algebraic sign organizes three qualitatively different spacetimes and three Penrose diagrams.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Complex-plane plot of the roots of Q moving as epsilon/m changes, synced to the three Penrose diagrams morphing into one another.

teaching_gems.gem: Present the maximal extension as a ladder of coordinate fixes, each removing one defect: static t -> EF tbar (horizon divergence) -> double null (conformal form) -> exponentials (zero at r_+) -> arctan (infinity).
teaching_gems.why_effective: Makes an intimidating transformation chain feel motivated and reusable for Kerr.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Stepper that applies each map to a grid of t = const and r = const curves and shows the image, ending in the Penrose block.

teaching_gems.gem: Diagnose incompleteness by comparing proper time with the diagram: a worldline that seems to crawl along a surface forever but reaches it in finite tau means the chart has ended, not the spacetime.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Gives learners a portable test for when to extend a manifold, tied back to the familiar Schwarzschild case.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Dual clocks (coordinate tbar and proper tau) on a particle approaching r_-; tau freezes at a finite value while tbar runs away.

teaching_gems.gem: Show infinite blueshift at the inner horizon by tracing light sent from ever later exterior times to an observer crossing r_-.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A purely causal Penrose-diagram argument produces a physical prediction (instability) without any perturbation theory.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Emit a ray each exterior 'year'; rays stack up on the traveller's worldline near r_-, with a frequency ratio readout climbing without bound.

gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Present the corrected relation and show the one-line derivation v - w = 2r*; verify numerically in the demo.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Exercise 19.12 prints ln(r^2 - 2mr - epsilon^2) for the super-extremal transformation; the argument must be r^2 - 2mr + epsilon^2 = Q.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Trapped surfaces, Cauchy horizons and instability are mentioned in a sentence each without definitions; the blueshift claim is called current research.

gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Define trapped surfaces by converging null normals, name r_- as a Cauchy horizon, and briefly note later work (mass inflation, strong cosmic censorship) with appropriate hedging.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The chart (19.31) is still degenerate at r_-, and the patching needed to build the full ladder is skipped; the rate constant is not identified as surface gravity.

tutor_notes: Opening question: 'If you add electric charge to a Schwarzschild black hole, what changes in g_00, and what would you expect near r = 0?' Let the learner guess the sign of the new term before revealing +epsilon^2/r^2.

Check prerequisites first: can the learner explain why r = 2m in Schwarzschild is a coordinate singularity and draw its EF and Penrose diagrams? If not, route back to DIV ch17-ch18 before this chapter.

Recommended order: (1) sketch g_00 for several epsilon/m; (2) classify by the discriminant; (3) causal character in each band; (4) light-cone slopes and EF diagram; (5) radial geodesics as potential motion; (6) incompleteness; (7) Kruskal-type coordinates and Penrose ladder; (8) interpretation and instability.

Give the physical intuition for the charge term early: the electric field carries positive energy spread outside any sphere, so the mass seen inside radius r is m - epsilon^2/2r; at small enough r this is negative, which is why the centre repels and the singularity is timelike.
Check for understanding: ask which coordinate is timelike at r = (r_+ + r_-)/2 and whether a rocket could hover there. Expected: r is timelike, hovering is impossible.
Check for understanding: ask the learner to predict the slope dtbar/dr of the outgoing ray at r = epsilon^2/2m (answer 1) and at the origin (answer -1) using only the definition of f.
Common learner question: 'Can you avoid the singularity?' Answer: yes, it is timelike, but you cannot go back out into your own universe; your future leads through r_- and then into a new exterior.
Common learner question: 'Why does the diagram show the particle never crossing r_-?' Answer via the Schwarzschild analogy (Fig. 17.7): finite proper time means the chart ends, not the spacetime.

When deriving Kruskal-type coordinates, first have the learner find the coefficient c = r_+^2/(r_+ - r_-) of ln(r - r_+) in r*; the exponential rate in (19.30) is 1/(2c), chosen so that exp(2 kappa r*) contains exactly one power of (r - r_+) to cancel the zero of g_00. That rate is the surface gravity of the outer horizon.
Flag the printed slips explicitly if the learner works Exercises 19.12 or 19.16: the logarithm in the super-extremal transformation needs +epsilon^2, and (19.32) should have unhalved exponents.

For advanced learners, connect the blueshift argument to the idea of a Cauchy horizon and mention, with hedging, later research on mass inflation and strong cosmic censorship; stress that the endless ladder of universes is not expected to survive realistic perturbations.
Keep units concrete for novices: an extremal solar-mass hole would need about 1.7e20 C, and real holes are essentially neutral, so RN is taught for its structure, which Kerr shares.
